title: Futures, Promises, std::async and Thread Pools
summary: A **future** is a handle to a result that will be available later. `std::async(f)` runs `f`, possibly on another thread, and returns a future; `get()` waits for the value, or rethrows the exception. A **promise** is the writing end of the same channel. `std::packaged_task` wraps a callable for use in thread pools.
ideas:
1. Start five `std::async` tasks with random sleeps and print each result as it becomes ready, using `wait_for`.
2. Use a `std::promise<void>` to release eight waiting threads at the same moment.
3. Type in the thread pool. Count primes in 100 chunks and add up the futures.

cards.q: What happens to an exception thrown inside a `std::async` task?
cards.a:
It is stored and rethrown when `get()` is called

The future carries either the result or the exception, so the caller handles it as if the call were local.

The default policy may defer the task, so nothing runs in parallel

With the default policy, the task may run lazily on the thread that calls `get()`. `std::launch::async` forces a new thread.

cards.q: Why must the future returned by `std::async` be kept?
cards.a:
Its destructor waits for the task, so a discarded future makes the call synchronous

The temporary future is destroyed at the end of the statement and blocks there until the task is finished.

cards.q: In the thread pool, why is the vector of workers the last member?
cards.a:
Destroyed first, the workers are joined while the queue still exists

The workers use the queue and the mutex. Declaring them last means they are destroyed first, while the others still exist.
